title: How the compiler tells overloads apart

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: Per this page, why does a class with `int getValue()` and `double getValue()` fail to compile?

options.text: Two methods of one class may never share one name
options.says: The page's whole subject is methods of one class sharing a name with different parameters.

options.text: A method returning double may not follow an int one
options.says: The page says nothing about declaration order; the clash is that the two signatures are the same.

options.text: The return type is not part of a method's signature
options.says: The page says Java tells overloads apart by name and parameter list, and the return type is not part of the signature.

questions.stem: Per this page, in what order does Java try to match a call to an overloaded method?

options.text: Exact type, then widening, then boxing, then varargs
options.says: The page lists exact match, type promotion, autoboxing and unboxing, then varargs.

options.text: Exact type, then boxing, then widening, then varargs
options.says: The page puts type promotion (widening) before autoboxing.

options.text: Exact type, then varargs, then widening, then boxing
options.says: The page puts varargs last, after promotion and boxing.

concepts: Java matches an overloaded call by exact type, then widening, then boxing, then varargs.
Methods that differ only in their return type do not compile, since the return type is not part of the signature.
